sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Vanaheimr** (Old Norse *Vanaheimr*, 'Van-home', from *Vana*, genitive plural of *Vanir*, + *heimr* 'home, world') is the homeland of the Vanir in Norse cosmology — the elder kindred of gods set beside the Æsir, keepers of fertility, wealth, peace, and the magic called seiðr. Its attestation is famously thin and exact: in *Vafþrúðnismál* 39 the wise powers (*vís regin*) shape [[njordr|Njörðr]] in Vanaheimr and give him to the gods as a hostage (*gísling*), with the promise that at the doom of the age he will come home among the wise Vanir.[^1] Snorri adds that Njörðr was raised in Vanaheimr before the exchange, and that his children [[freyr|Freyr]] and [[freyja|Freyja]] share his double citizenship.[^2] Beyond this the record is silent: no surviving poem is set in Vanaheimr, no traveller describes it, and the realm is known entirely through its exiles and through the war whose peace made the two kindreds one household.[^3]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Vanaheimr** — identical to the ASCII input, because normalized Old Norse writes no diacritic in this compound. The mechanical rule therefore places the name in Tier 2: nothing distinctive is lost in transit, a statement about orthography and never about the realm. The temple is domain-less: the plain-ASCII vanaheimr.com is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release.

sources.citation: Vafþrúðnismál 39 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 23, ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Vanaheimr, Vanir.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Old Norse as **Vanaheimr** — a transparent compound of *Vana*, the genitive plural of *Vanir*, and *heimr* 'home, world, dwelling-place', the same second element as in [[alfheimr|Álfheimr]] and the whole heimr-family of cosmological homesteads. Vafþrúðnismál 39 preserves the dative form *í Vanaheimi*.

The etymology of the first element is one of the honest open questions of the onomasticon. *Vanir* has been connected with Old Norse *vinr* 'friend', with a root of 'striving, winning', and with Latin *Venus* — none secure, and de Vries registers the proposals without settling them.[^1] What is not disputed is the compound's transparency to a medieval speaker: the home of the Vanir, as Álfheimr is the home of the elves.

The ASCII form is not a fallback here but the form itself: normalized Old Norse writes nine plain Latin letters and a capital. The Unicode restoration **Vanaheimr** therefore preserves nothing the ASCII alphabet loses, and the mechanical rule classifies the name Tier 2 — an orthographic fact, not a judgment on the realm.[^2]

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **v** → **V** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **e** → **e** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **m** → **m** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same

The project holds no domain for this name. The plain-ASCII **vanaheimr.com** is registered to a third party outside the collection and is watched for release; this temple claims nothing it does not hold.[^3]

sources.citation: de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Vanir, heimr.

Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Vanir, heimr; Zoëga, Geir T., A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Vanir, heimr.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈwɑ.nɑˌhɛi̯mr/** — Old Norse Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **Va-** — Initial labial-velar glide [w], not modern [v]: Old Norse initial v continued Proto-Germanic *w and was still a glide in the classical period; the stressed vowel is short open [ɑ]
- **-na-** — Voiced alveolar nasal [n] and a second short open [ɑ]; both vowels of Vana- are short, the manuscripts writing no length mark
- **-heimr** — The rising diphthong [ɛi̯] of heimr, then bilabial [m] and the tapped or trilled [r] of the masculine nominative ending, fully sounded

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'WAH-nah-HAYM-r' — begin with a w as in 'water', keep both a's short and open, glide the -hei- as in 'hay', and finish with a light rolled r.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Old Norse** — Vanaheimr, with the dative í Vanaheimi attested in Vafþrúðnismál 39
- **Younger Futhark** — ᚢᛅᚾᚼᛁᛘᛁᚱ (u-a-n-h-i-m-i-r), the Viking-Age runic rendering, initial /w/ written with úr
- **Modern Scandinavian** — Swedish and Danish Vanahem, Modern Icelandic Vanaheimur, the learned form kept alive from the medieval corpus
- **Other Germanic** — none: the Vanir are attested only in the Norse sources, so no cognate realm-name exists in Old English or Gothic[^2]

Vanaheimr is Tier 2 because the restoration preserves nothing the ASCII form loses: no diacritic, no distinctive letter, no vowel length. English and Old Norse write the name identically.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
de Vries, Jan, Altnordisches etymologisches Wörterbuch, 2nd ed. (Leiden: Brill, 1962), s.v. Vanir (the Norse-only attestation of the kindred).

sections.label: Original Script & Provenance
sections.purpose: Original writing system, transliteration steps, uncertainty markers, font/display notes.
sections.body:
The name is preserved in medieval Icelandic manuscripts in the Latin alphabet as **Vanaheimr** — Old Norse (North Germanic), attested 13th c. CE in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (Vafþrúðnismál, with the dative í Vanaheimi) and the codices of Snorri's Edda, recording material centuries older.[^1] Before the Latin bookhand, Old Norse names were carved in the Younger Futhark; no runic attestation of this compound survives, so the manuscript form is the primary witness. The runic rendering is **ᚢᛅᚾᚼᛁᛘᛁᚱ** (u-a-n-h-i-m-i-r).

The scholarly rendering proceeds step by step:

- ᚢ (úr) writes the rounded back vowels /u, o, ø, ǫ, y/ and /w/; the initial /v/ of the normalized spelling continues Proto-Germanic *w- and is represented by úr.
- ᛅ (ár) writes /a/, /á/ and /æ/; ᚾ (nauðr) writes /n/.
- The spelling uanhimir is a normalized phonetic reconstruction; Younger Futhark does not distinguish voiced/voiceless stops or separate short and long vowels.
- The compound is transparent — Vana (genitive plural of Vanir) + heimr 'home, world' — and the normalized Old Norse form writes no diacritic: both a's are short, and no distinctive letter (þ, ð, æ, ǫ) occurs in the name.
- The Unicode restoration Vanaheimr is therefore identical to the ASCII form — the restoration is a matter of canonical reference, not rescued orthography.[^2]

sources.citation: Barnes, Michael P., Runes: A Handbook (Woodbridge: Boydell, 2012); Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957).
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Vanir, heimr; Zoëga, A Concise Dictionary of Old Icelandic (Clarendon Press, 1910), s.v. Vanir, heimr.

sections.label: Domains & Attributes
sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
**Vanaheimr** is catalogued under Home of the Vanir — and the title is the whole dossier: the sources define the realm by its people and its role in the peace, never by landscape, buildings, or events within it.[^1]

### The Vanir's Country

The homeland of the elder kindred — [[njordr|Njörðr]], [[freyr|Freyr]], [[freyja|Freyja]] — the gods of growth, wealth, peace, and seiðr, whom the corpus consistently presents as a separate people with their own customs, down to marriage law the Æsir forbade and the Vanir practised.

### The Hostage's Home

Vanaheimr's one mythic act is a departure: the wise powers shape Njörðr there and hand him to the Æsir as the gísling, the hostage who seals the peace after the first war in the world — and Vafþrúðnismál promises him a homecoming at the doom of the age.

### The Undefeated Enemy

In Völuspá's account it is the Vanir who break the wall of Ásgarðr and tread the field in victory — the only power in the corpus that breaches the Æsir's defences by open war. Vanaheimr is the country strong enough to stalemate heaven and wise enough to settle it.

### The Wise Powers

The realm's inhabitants are named only by their wisdom — vís regin, 'the wise powers', in Vafþrúðnismál; the war-wise Vanir in Völuspá — a people the tradition never describes but always respects.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 23, trans. Faulkes (1987); Vafþrúðnismál 39 and Völuspá 21–24 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
No Viking-Age image can be securely read as a picture of Vanaheimr, so the realm's symbolic vocabulary is built from the events and objects the texts attach to the Vanir and the peace:[^1]

- **The hostage pledge (gísling)** — Njörðr's transfer to the Æsir: peace made by exchanging what each side could not bear to lose
- **The vat of the truce** — the vessel into which both kindreds spat to seal the peace, from which Kvasir was made: reconciliation given a body[^1]
- **Sheaf and ship** — the Vanir's twin wealth: the harvest of the fields and the sea-borne fortune of Njörðr of Nóatún and Freyr's Skíðblaðnir[^2]
- **The seiðr-staff** — the magic [[freyja|Freyja]] first taught among the Æsir, which Ynglinga saga says was Vanir custom: power the immigrants carried from home[^1]
- **The broken wall of Ásgarðr** — the Vanir's victory in the field, the one breach of the Æsir's defences the corpus records[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 4 (the peace vat and Kvasir; the hostage exchange; seiðr as Vanir custom), trans. Lee M. Hollander (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1964).
Völuspá 21–24 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014); Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 23–24, trans. Faulkes (1987).

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Vanaheimr has no myth of its own: no surviving story is set inside it, no traveller describes it, no poem is located there. Its whole mythology is told from outside, by and about the gods who left it.

### In Vanaheimr the Wise Powers Created Him (Vafþrúðnismál 39)

In the wisdom-contest with the giant Vafþrúðnir, [[odinn|Óðinn]] asks whence [[njordr|Njörðr]] came among the sons of the Æsir, he who rules so many temples and sanctuaries though he was not raised among the Æsir. The giant's answer is the realm's one great attestation: in Vanaheimr the wise powers created him and gave him to the gods as a hostage — and at the doom of the age he will come back home among the wise Vanir. The stanza names the realm, explains Njörðr's double citizenship, and promises a homecoming the surviving corpus never narrates.[^1]

### The First War in the World (Völuspá 21–24)

The seeress remembers the world's first war: Gullveig, the thrice-burned, thrice-born witch, is speared and burned in Hárr's hall yet lives; the gods take counsel whether the Æsir should pay tribute; and when battle is joined it is the Vanir who break the wall of Ásgarðr and tread the field in victory — the war-wise people. No poem says who won in the end, and the silence is the point: the war could not be won, and what follows in every account is not conquest but exchange.[^2]

### The Hostage Exchange (Gylfaginning 23; Ynglinga saga 4)

The Vanir gave their foremost: Njörðr, raised in Vanaheimr, and with him his son [[freyr|Freyr]]. The Æsir gave Hœnir, thought fit to be a chieftain, and with him [[mimir|Mímir]], wisest of men, and Kvasir. When Hœnir proved helpless in council without Mímir at his shoulder, the Vanir reckoned themselves cheated, cut off Mímir's head, and sent it to Óðinn, who preserved it with herbs and spells and consults it for hidden lore. Njörðr and Freyr thrived among the Æsir — so naturalized that [[loki|Loki]] must taunt Njörðr with being only a hostage sent from the east — while the Vanir kept their country and the corpus keeps the asymmetry forever unreconciled.[^3]

### Vanaland by the Tanais (Ynglinga saga 1)

Snorri's Heimskringla opens its euhemerized geography with the river the medieval world called the Tanais — the Don — and names the country on its eastern side Vanaland or Vanaheimr, and the river itself Vanakvísl: the mythic homeland become a border province of legendary history, the starting point of the migration that carries Óðinn's people north to found the Yngling dynasty at [[uppsala|Uppsala]]. Even euhemerized, the pattern holds: Vanaheimr is the place one leaves to found dynasties elsewhere.[^4]

sources.citation: Vafþrúðnismál 39 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Völuspá 21–24 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 23, trans. Faulkes (1987); Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 4, trans. Hollander (1964); Lokasenna 34 (Poetic Edda).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 1, trans. Hollander (1964).

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Vanaheimr's interpretive life is the Vanir problem itself: why does one mythology keep two divine kindreds? Dumézil made the pairing the cornerstone of his comparative system — the Æsir holding sovereignty and war, the Vanir fecundity and wealth, their war and merger the mythic charter of a complete pantheon, with structural cousins in Rome's pairing of the Di Indigetes with the immigrant Di Novensides and in kindred patterns across the Indo-European record.[^1]

Current handbooks are cooler. The Vanir are attested only in the Norse sources — no Old English or Gothic trace of the kindred survives; the Æsir/Vanir boundary blurs in practice, since [[skadi|Skaði]] is a giant's daughter numbered among the goddesses and Njörðr's children outshine their host kindred; and the war's mythology may encode history, ritual, or pure narrative logic in proportions no source will let us measure.[^2] What stands cleanly is the corpus's own testimony: two kindreds, one war, one exchange, and a homeland that keeps its identity through its exiles. Within the corpus, the realm's household and kin are [[njordr|Njörðr]], [[freyr|Freyr]], [[freyja|Freyja]], [[skadi|Skaði]], and the hostage-counterpart [[mimir|Mímir]].

sources.citation: Dumézil, Georges, Gods of the Ancient Northmen, ed. Einar Haugen (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1973).

Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Vanir, Vanaheimr; Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Vanir; Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Vanir, Æsir–Vanir war.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body:
Vanaheimr's modern life follows the Vanir's. Nineteenth-century philology made the Æsir–Vanir war a scholarly crux — historicized as a memory of clashing cults, read by Dumézil as structural myth — and the debate remains the standard introduction to how hard it is to get history out of the Eddas.[^1] Modern Heathenry restored the kindred to practice: Vanatrú names a living devotional current centred on Njörðr, Freyr, and Freyja as gods of peace, fertility, and the household's wealth, with Vanaheimr honoured as their true home.[^2]

Popular culture adopted the realm as scenery: Marvel's Thor comics placed Vanaheim among the Nine Realms and carried it onto film, and Santa Monica Studio's God of War Ragnarök (2022) rendered it as a vast jungle river-world — depictions with no warrant in the medieval record, which gives the realm no landscape at all.[^3] The restoration keeps the plain compound the sources actually wrote: the Vanir's home, named once in a wisdom-contest and remembered ever since.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Vanir, Æsir–Vanir war.
von Schnurbein, Stefanie, Norse Revival: Transformations of Germanic Neopaganism (Leiden: Brill, 2016).
Santa Monica Studio, God of War Ragnarök (2022); Marvel Comics, the Thor titles (Vanaheim among the Nine Realms).

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body:
A realm named once in a wisdom-contest can leave no votives: Vanaheimr's evidence is manuscript evidence. Vafþrúðnismál and Völuspá survive in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270), and Snorri's Gylfaginning and the Heimskringla tradition transmit the prose attestations. No runic inscription names Vanaheimr, and none names the Vanir as a kindred — a silence the realm shares with most of the cosmological furniture.

The material record belongs to the Vanir's cult rather than their home. Adam of Bremen's description (c. 1070s) of the temple at [[uppsala|Uppsala]] sets the idol Fricco — [[freyr|Freyr]] — between Wodan and [[thor|Thor]], fashioned with an immense phallus as the god of peace and pleasure: the Vanir's nearest contemporary portrait.[^1] The dense stratum of Scandinavian place-names compounded with [[njordr|Njörðr]] and Freyr — Swedish Närlunda from *Njarðarlundr*, Frøslev, Frösåker and their kin — maps the kindred's worship across the landscape even where the mythology is silent, though the distribution is uneven enough that no simple map of a 'Vanir religion' survives scrutiny.[^2] The Yngling dynasty's claimed descent from Yngvi-Freyr ties that cult geography to the great burial mounds of Gamla Uppsala — the closest the earth comes to showing us Vanaheimr's people.[^3]

sources.citation: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum IV.26–27, trans. Francis J. Tschan (New York: Columbia University Press, 1959).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Njörðr, Freyr (the place-name evidence).
Brink, Stefan, 'How Uniform Was the Old Norse Religion?', in The Viking World, ed. Stefan Brink and Neil Price (London: Routledge, 2008).

sections.label: Poetic Edda
sections.body:
The Poetic Edda holds all three of Vanaheimr's direct attestations, and together they are the whole record. *Vafþrúðnismál* 39 is the charter: asked by the disguised [[odinn|Óðinn]] whence [[njordr|Njörðr]] came among the sons of the Æsir, the giant answers that in Vanaheimr the wise powers created him and gave him to the gods as a hostage, and that at the doom of the age he will come home among the wise Vanir — the stanza that names the realm, explains the god's double citizenship, and promises a return no surviving poem narrates.[^1]

*Völuspá* 21–24 supplies the war that made the exchange necessary: Gullveig thrice burned and thrice reborn in Hárr's hall, the council on tribute, the battle joined, and the Vanir — the war-wise people — breaking the wall of Ásgarðr and treading the field. The poem never says who won; it only says the world had never known war before this one.[^2]

And *Lokasenna* 34 gives the long afterlife of the settlement in a single taunt: [[loki|Loki]] reminds Njörðr that he was sent from the east as a hostage to the gods — generations of naturalization cancelled in one line, the immigrant's origin thrown back at him in the Æsir's own hall.[^3]

sources.citation: Vafþrúðnismál 39 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Völuspá 21–24 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Lokasenna 34 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Prose Edda
sections.body:
Snorri's Edda gives Vanaheimr its prose frame. Gylfaginning 23, the chapter on [[njordr|Njörðr]], states the fact plainly: Njörðr was raised in Vanaheimr, and the Vanir gave him to the Æsir as a hostage in the peace exchange, receiving Hœnir in return. The same chapter plants the realm's distinctiveness in law and custom: among the Vanir, Snorri says, marriage between brother and sister was lawful, and Njörðr's children [[freyr|Freyr]] and [[freyja|Freyja]] were born of such a union before the exchange — a custom the Æsir forbade, and one of the few places the corpus lets the two kindreds differ in more than name.[^1]

Skáldskaparmál keeps the affiliation alive in the poets' shorthand: Njörðr's standard kennings style him god of the Vanir, and the hostage settlement underlies his standing among the Æsir throughout the kenning system. Snorri's ordering deserves note — Njörðr's chapter follows the ásynja catalogue and precedes Freyr and Freyja's, so that the Edda's own architecture tells the story of immigration: the father first, naturalized and temple-rich, then the children who will outshine the host kindred.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 23, trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál (kennings for Njörðr), trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Viking Society for Northern Research, 1998).

sections.label: Runic Evidence
sections.body:
The runic corpus contains no attestation of Vanaheimr and none of the Vanir as a kindred. No runestone names the realm, no inscription invokes Njörðr or Freyr by their kindred's name, and the compound belongs wholly to the manuscript tradition — a silence the realm shares with nearly all the cosmological place-names of the Eddas.[^1]

What can be said runologically is the rendering itself: in the Younger Futhark the name would have been carved ᚢᛅᚾᚼᛁᛘᛁᚱ (u-a-n-h-i-m-i-r), with the initial /w/ written by úr, the rune that writes the rounded back vowels and /w/. The sixteen-rune row underspecifies nothing this name needs distinguished — it carries no diacritic, and its consonants are all unambiguous in the short-twig system — so the runic and manuscript witnesses would agree letter for letter. No Viking-Age carving of the name is known; the Eddas' spelling remains the primary witness.[^2]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Vanir, Vanaheimr (the limits of attestation).
Barnes, Michael P., Runes: A Handbook (Woodbridge: Boydell, 2012); Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor (Clarendon Press, 1957), runic appendix.

sections.label: Sagas & Medieval Sources
sections.body:
In the saga corpus Vanaheimr becomes legendary history. Snorri's Ynglinga saga opens with the river the medieval world called the Tanais — the Don — and places Vanaland or Vanaheimr on its eastern side, with the river itself named Vanakvísl: the mythic homeland set down as a real border country, the far eastern starting point of the migration that brings [[odinn|Óðinn]]'s people north to Sweden and the Yngling kings to [[uppsala|Uppsala]].[^1]

Ynglinga saga 4 then tells the war and the peace as history. The Æsir and the Vanir fight to exhaustion and make peace by exchanging hostages: the Vanir give their foremost men, Njörðr the Wealthy and his son [[freyr|Freyr]]; the Æsir give Hœnir, declaring him fit to be a chieftain, and send [[mimir|Mímir]], wisest of men, in exchange for Kvasir, wisest of the Vanir. When Hœnir answers every council with 'let others decide' in Mímir's absence, the Vanir reckon themselves cheated, behead Mímir, and send the head to Óðinn, who smears it with herbs and chants over it so that it speaks hidden lore to him. The same chapter credits Freyja with teaching the Æsir seiðr, 'as was the custom among the Vanir' — the saga's way of saying that the deepest magic in the Æsir's arsenal is an import from Vanaheimr.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 1, trans. Lee M. Hollander (Austin: University of Texas Press, 1964).
Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Ynglinga saga 4, trans. Hollander (1964).

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Every heimr in the Norse cosmos is a homestead, but Vanaheimr is the one defined by leaving it. Ásgarðr has its walls and halls, [[midgardr|Miðgarðr]] its fence, Jötunheimr its giants; Vanaheimr has a departure and a promise. The wise powers shape [[njordr|Njörðr]] and hand him over, and the corpus never once takes us back across the border — we know the realm only as the place the hostage came from, the address on a homecoming that Ragnarǫk will finally honour.[^1]

There is something exact in that economy: a peace that could only be made by each side surrendering what it could least spare, and a god who spends his whole mythic life as a guest in someone else's heaven, ruling temples among the Æsir while remaining, at the level of grammar and fate, a Vanir abroad. Vanaheimr is the mythology's quietest lesson in what homes are for: not to be described, but to be owed a return.[^1]

sources.citation: Vafþrúðnismál 39 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
